html:
Surah Al-Falaq (The Daybreak) is the 113th surah of the Qur’an — five short verses, Makkī by the dominant classification of Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, with a minority Madanī opinion rooted in the surah’s linked occasion of revelation with Surah an-Nās. Together with an-Nās it forms al-Muʿawwidhatān — the “Two Refuges” — the paired closing of the Qur’an that the Prophet ﷺ took as his nightly protection and after every obligatory prayer. The structural pairing is deliberate and total: where an-Nās teaches refuge from the internal whisper of al-Waswās al-Khannās, Al-Falaq teaches refuge from the external harms of the created world. The surah names four categories in ascending specificity — the generic evil of all created things (sharr mā khalaq), the evil of darkness when it settles in (ghāsiq idhā waqab), the evil of the women who blow on knots (al-naffāthāt fil-ʿuqad, sorcery), and the evil of the envier when he envies (ḥāsid idhā ḥasad). Al-Qurṭubī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur’an argues this is an exhaustive formula — every external harm that can touch a human being falls within one of the four categories, and the opening clause sharr mā khalaq names them collectively before the three particulars are singled out for their severity. The refuge is thus structural, not emotional: the believer is taught to classify the harm before invoking the Refuge.

Ibn Kathīr opens the surah with the lexical range of al-falaq itself. The dominant reading, from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, is daybreak — the splitting of the night by the first light, chosen as the Lord-name here because dawn is the archetype of Allah’s power to split open what is sealed. A secondary reading, also from Ibn ʿAbbās, extends falaq to everything Allah splits open — the seed from which the plant emerges, the womb from which the child comes, the mountain split by the stream. The semantic range is theologically precise: the One asked for refuge is the One who continuously splits open every closed thing by His decree, including the closed hearts of sorcerers and enviers whose malice is itself a closed thing He can open. The surah’s opening Lord-name is therefore not decorative; it is the reason the refuge is granted. Ibn al-Qayyim in Badā’iʿ al-Fawā’id builds on this: the Qur’an pairs each refuge with the Lord-name that most directly answers the specific evil, and Rabb al-Falaq answers evil as containment — what is bound, Allah unbinds; what is tied, Allah unties.

The explicit naming of sorcery — al-naffāthāt fil-ʿuqad, “those who blow on knots” — is deliberate and classical scholars treat it as the surah’s doctrinal center. Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā argues the explicit naming is Allah’s rebuttal of every opinion — ancient and modern — that denies the reality of siḥr or treats it as mere psychological suggestion. The verse addresses the ritual specifics of the sorcery of the time: a female witch would tie knots in a cord while blowing (nafth) a mixture of saliva and incantation into each knot, binding the victim through the physical bond. The Qur’an names this practice and places it in the refuge formula — confirming that sorcery is real as a harm that can afflict the body (though it cannot alter the heart’s faith or the mind’s testimony), and that its remedy is not counter-magic but refuge in the One who splits open all knots. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr both note that the fourth category — the envier — is distinguished from the sorcerer because envy (ḥasad) is itself a cause of sorcery: the envier may not himself tie knots, but his gaze and wish can harm the envied through the same mechanism Allah established, which is why the surah names both the practitioner and the motivator.

The authentic practice of the Prophet ﷺ with Al-Falaq is the same firm hadith ground as its pair an-Nās. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5017 records ʿĀ’ishah: the Prophet ﷺ would cup his hands every night, blow into them, recite the three Quls (Ikhlāṣ, Falaq, Nās), and wipe over his body three times — nightly, not occasionally. Sunan al-Nasā’ī 5430 (with a parallel in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 814), from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, carries the Prophet’s ﷺ unqualified praise: “Have you not seen the verses that have been revealed to me tonight, the like of which has never been seen before? Qul aʿūdhu bi-Rabbi al-falaq and Qul aʿūdhu bi-Rabbi al-nās.” Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2903 (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ) and Sunan Abī Dāwūd 1523 (ṣaḥīḥ per al-Albānī in Ṣaḥīḥ Sunan Abī Dāwūd) record the Prophet’s ﷺ command to ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir to recite the Muʿawwidhāt after every obligatory prayer. The authentic baseline is beyond dispute: the surah is not reserved for emergencies, it is daily armor.

The shared occasion of revelation for Al-Falaq and an-Nās is the sorcery incident of Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam, narrated in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5763, 3268 and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2189. Labīd, a Jewish man of Madinah, cast a spell on the Prophet ﷺ using strands of his hair tied into a comb and deposited in a well. Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ of the location and the two surahs were revealed as the cure — one verse per knot, each of the eleven knots untying as its verse was recited. The hadith is in both Ṣaḥīḥs, and the historical event is why the pair is called al-Muʿawwidhatān. There is an honest minority dissent to record: historically, the Muʿtazilah rejected the Labīd narration as incompatible with the Prophet’s ﷺ ʿiṣmah (infallibility), arguing that if the Prophet ﷺ could be affected by sorcery then his conveyance of revelation could not be trusted. The mainstream Sunni response, most fully developed in Ibn Ḥajar’s Fatḥ al-Bārī (commentary on Bukhārī 5763), draws a hard line: the Prophet’s ﷺ ʿiṣmah in tablīgh (the transmission of revelation) is absolute, but his bashariyyah (humanity) means his body can be afflicted like any other human body. The sorcery affected him in matters of worldly perception (he reportedly imagined doing things he had not done), not in matters of revelation. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ in al-Shifā and Ibn Taymiyyah elsewhere offer the same distinction. The Muʿtazilī rejection is thus a doctrinal objection, not a ḥadīth-criticism objection — the chain is ṣaḥīḥ and the tawthiq is universal. Where the Qur’an itself (Al-Falaq v. 4) names sorcery as a reality from which refuge is sought, denying its effect on the Prophet ﷺ’s body is denying the surah’s own premise.

The practical fiqh of the surah mirrors its pair. Recite Al-Falaq with an-Nās and al-Ikhlāṣ three times after Fajr and Maghrib, and once after Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, and ʿIshā’ — the practice recorded in Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5082 and Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 3575 from ʿAbdullāh ibn Khubayb (ḥasan per al-Albānī). Recite them before sleep with the Bukhārī 5017 blowing-and-wiping method. Recite them as ruqyah when sick, as ʿĀ’ishah did for the Prophet ﷺ in his final illness (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5735, 5751). The surah is not a charm — it has no efficacy divorced from the believer’s submission to the Lord of the Daybreak. Its power is theological: it names the four categories of external evil, names the One who splits open what evil has sealed, and binds the two together in a formula so complete that the Prophet ﷺ said — and the chain is ṣaḥīḥ — “No one asks for refuge with the likes of them.”

sources.label: Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr — Surah Al-Falaq
sources.note: lexical range of al-falaq (daybreak / splitting-open of all creation per Ibn ʿAbbās + Mujāhid), four-category refuge structure, and the distinction between the sorcerer (al-naffāthāt) and the envier (al-ḥāsid) as separate but linked categories

sources.label: al-Qurṭubī — al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur’an
sources.note: exhaustive-formula reading of the four categories (sharr mā khalaq as the collective, three particulars for severity); the lexical treatment of ghāsiq idhā waqab (night-fall), naffāthāt fil-ʿuqad (knot-blowing sorcery), and ḥāsid idhā ḥasad (envier when he envies)

sources.label: Ibn Taymiyyah — Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā
sources.note: defense of the explicit Qur’anic naming of sorcery against denial of its reality; argument that siḥr can afflict the body but cannot alter faith or testimony; refuge-in-the-One-who-splits-knots as the only legitimate remedy (not counter-magic)

sources.label: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5017 + 5763 / 3268; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2189
sources.note: the three-Quls nightly protection sunnah (5017: cupping hands, blowing, reciting Ikhlāṣ-Falaq-Nās, wiping body three times); the Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam sorcery incident as shared occasion of revelation for the Muʿawwidhatān (5763/3268 and Muslim 2189)

sources.label: Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī — Fatḥ al-Bārī bi-Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī
sources.note: commentary on Bukhārī 5763 — the hard distinction between ʿiṣmah in tablīgh (absolute) and bashariyyah (bodily affection permitted) that answers the Muʿtazilī doctrinal objection to the Labīd narration; parallel treatment from al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ in al-Shifā
